title: Percentage and Percentage Change
scientificNotes: General competitive-exam quantitative-aptitude topic; included to match the exam's Part A scope.
explanation: A percentage expresses a quantity as a fraction of 100, making comparison across different totals straightforward. Percentage CHANGE compares a new value to an OLD (original) value — always divide by the OLD value, never the new one, since percentage change is defined relative to the starting point. For SUCCESSIVE percentage changes (e.g. a price rises 10% then falls 10%), the changes do NOT cancel out — they must be applied one after another to the running value, not added/subtracted directly, because the second percentage is taken of a DIFFERENT base than the first.

variables.meaning: The quantity being expressed as a percentage

workedExample.scenario: A price of ₹200 rises by 10%, then the new price falls by 10%. Find the final price.
workedExample.result: Final price = ₹198 (NOT back to ₹200 — a net 1% decrease)

commonMistakes: Assuming a percentage increase followed by an equal percentage decrease returns to the original value — it does not, because the decrease is applied to the ALREADY-INCREASED (larger) value, so the net effect is always a decrease for equal-magnitude successive changes.
Computing percentage change by dividing the difference by the NEW value instead of the OLD (original) value.
genZNote: Successive percentage changes don't cancel — a +10% then −10% still leaves you down 1%, because the second cut takes a bigger bite in absolute terms.
